summary.text: A 71-year-old hemodialysis-dependent woman with end-stage renal disease from diabetic kidney disease, hypertension, hypothyroidism, type 2 diabetes mellitus and coronary artery disease on clopidogrel had essential thrombocythemia diagnosed three years earlier with an MPL W515L mutation and was on hydroxyurea. One month before admission she had an acute NSTEMI treated with drug-eluting stents, and aspirin was added.

She presented to the emergency department with one week of progressively worsening dyspnea and chest tightness. Examination showed distant heart sounds and cold extremities; the chest X-ray showed a water-bottle heart, CT a massive pericardial effusion, and echocardiography a large effusion over 2 cm with diastolic right ventricular collapse, consistent with cardiac tamponade. Hemorrhagic cardiac tamponade was diagnosed.

Ultrasound-guided pericardiocentesis yielded 800 mL of hemorrhagic fluid and a further 1400 mL drained over three days. Aspirin was discontinued. Fluid cultures were negative and cytology showed no malignant cells; platelet function closure times were prolonged. A repeat echocardiogram on hospital day 6 confirmed resolution of the effusion, and she was discharged on hospital day 20 on clopidogrel monotherapy.

Six months after the first hospitalization she had another NSTEMI with in-stent stenosis treated by drug-eluting balloon angioplasty. Cilostazol was added to clopidogrel, although the report describes its timing inconsistently. Eight months after the second hospitalization a further NSTEMI with in-stent restenosis was again treated with drug-eluting balloon angioplasty.

Twelve months after the third hospitalization she suddenly lost consciousness, and the electrocardiogram in the emergency department showed pulse ventricular tachycardia. Considering her multiple comorbidities, her family decided against cardioversion, and the patient died.
